questions.q: What is the literal description of the mark on the wall as given in the opening paragraph of the essay?
questions.a:
The mark is described as a small round mark, black upon the white wall, about six or seven inches above the mantelpiece.  
A wrong answer (e.g., "a nail hole" or "a snail") reveals the student has confused the narrator's later speculations with the initial literal observation. The text explicitly states the mark's physical appearance before any interpretation begins.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator says, "If that mark was made by a nail, it can't have been for a picture; it must have been for a miniature."
questions.a:
The narrator infers the mark is too small and round for a regular picture nail, so it must have held a miniature portrait. This shows the narrator's mind making rapid, imaginative deductions from a tiny detail.  
A wrong answer that treats this as a fact (e.g., "The previous owners hung a miniature there") reveals the student cannot distinguish the narrator's speculative fancy from textual reality. The phrase "I don't believe it was made by a nail after all" later confirms it was speculation.

questions.q: Apply the literal/inferential distinction to this question: "What does the narrator compare the speed of life to?" Provide the literal comparison and one inference about why she chooses that image.
questions.a:
Literal: Life is compared to "being blown through the Tube at fifty miles an hour — landing at the other end without a single hairpin in one's hair."  
Inference: The Tube (London Underground) image suggests modern, mechanised, uncontrollable speed and the loss of personal adornments (hairpins) symbolises how civilisation strips away our illusions of control.  
A wrong answer that only quotes the comparison without explaining its significance shows the student can retrieve literal information but cannot make the inferential leap to thematic meaning.

questions.q: Analyse the narrator's attitude toward "generalisations" and "Whitaker's Table of Precedency" in the middle section. How does her tone shift from literal description to inferential critique of social structures?
questions.a:
Literally, she describes generalisations as having a "military sound" recalling "leading articles, cabinet ministers" and Sunday rituals like tapestry tablecloths. Inferentially, she critiques these as "half phantoms" — socially constructed rules mistaken for absolute reality. The shift occurs when she calls the damnation for disbelieving them "only a sense of illegitimate freedom," revealing her view that social hierarchies (Whitaker's Table) are arbitrary mental constructs.  
A wrong answer that merely lists the examples (Sunday walks, tablecloths) without analysing the shift from description to philosophical critique shows inability to trace the narrator's inferential reasoning.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the essay's ending: the mark turns out to be a snail. Does this literal resolution undermine or reinforce the inferential journey? Justify with textual evidence.
questions.a:
It reinforces the journey. The snail's mundane reality ("Ah, the mark on the wall! It was a snail...") contrasts with the vast philosophical speculations it provoked, illustrating Woolf's central idea: the mind's "flight of ideas" is more significant than the external trigger. The narrator's final return to "wood... trees... peaceful thoughts" shows she values the thinking process over the object.  
A wrong answer claiming the ending makes the essay "pointless" reveals a misunderstanding of modernist stream-of-consciousness: the mark's triviality is the point — it demonstrates how minor stimuli unleash major mental landscapes.

questions.q: Create an inferential question about the "colonel and the clergy" passage (paragraph on South Downs barrows) that requires synthesising at least two textual clues about the narrator's view of scholarship.
questions.a:
Sample question: "What does the narrator's imaginary portrait of the antiquary — retired colonel, arrow-head comparisons, pamphlet cut short by a stroke — suggest about her attitude toward academic knowledge?"  
A good answer synthesises: (1) the colonel's trivial pursuit (arrow-heads, plum jam) and (2) his death mid-pamphlet with "last conscious thoughts... of the camp and that arrow-head" to infer that the narrator sees specialised scholarship as a futile, self-enclosed game disconnected from living thought.  
A poor answer that merely summarises the colonel's activities shows the student cannot generate an inference requiring synthesis of character details and authorial tone.
